cells.tense: The ending is here and you can stand in it with the people it touches, steadying the space while it closes.
cells.ask: Build the goodbye that outlasts it. Choose a shape the closing can take — a meal, a final walk, a box set on the step — and carry it out. Make it solid enough to stand on afterwards.
cells.core:
Things end around you, and you stay steady in the middle of it. You can hold a room while it breaks without turning brittle or going under, and the ones who lean on you feel exactly that: you don't rush them past the hurt, and your own footing doesn't slip.

What's left is the goodbye itself. Choose a shape the closing can take — a meal, a final walk, a box set on the step — and carry it out. That is the builder's move: you make something solid enough to stand on after the ending. Nothing has to be carried past the doing, and once it's made you can set it down finished.

Now the ending has a shape, and you didn't have to force anyone to feel it.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold the goodbyes and stay standing.
cells.verb: holding space for what's ending without going down with it
cells.place: at the edge of something you loved, keeping it steady while it ends

cells.tense: You are already braced for the next ending, closing it in your head before it has finished closing here.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Release this ending, not a later one. Take something already over — a tie you keep loosening for someone gone — and let it rest as finished. See what you kept it for. Keep that much.
cells.core:
You can see the ending coming long before it arrives, and you have started clearing the decks for it. Some part of you believes the break can be pre-absolved if you get ahead of it — and the people still eating dinner with you are watching you end something that hasn't finished leaving.

Let it end here first. Take something already over — a tie you keep loosening for someone who has left, a habit of checking on something that closed last winter — and let it rest as finished. See what you kept it for, and keep that much. The rest can go.

It will end in its own time. You are not the one who has to call it early.
cells.sheetLine: You're grieving on schedule before the loss has happened.
cells.verb: holding space for what's ending without going down with it
cells.place: at the edge of something you loved, keeping it steady while it ends

cells.tense: The ending happened while you were still at the door, telling yourself you had not come through it yet.
cells.act: say the hard thing gently, once
cells.ask: Offer one true sentence into the quiet it left. Say it slowly, aloud if you can — even just to yourself. Nothing has to happen after it.
cells.core:
The break already happened, and you are still where the room used to be, not bringing yourself to say so. Speaking of it has gone quiet in you — to the people around, to yourself — and the clearing has slowed to a stop around your silence. You have not come through the door yet, not because the ending is unfinished, but because you have not said it.

One sentence is enough. Say the hard thing gently, once, in your own words — that it's over, that you miss it, that you are standing in a room already bare. Say it aloud if you can, even to yourself. Nothing has to follow it.

The door was behind you already. The sentence is what lets you turn and face where you're standing.

cells.tense: You are clearing things for everyone around you and calling it staying out of it, pen down in a room you are already writing.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Cut to a clean line. Mark something finished in a plain sentence, then act on it the same day — no second-guessing, nothing explained away.
cells.core:
You are the one who sees what needs to close before the others can — and your account of yourself is that you are only keeping the peace while it closes. You are the keeper of the endings, and you have been calling yourself a bystander. The person who moves things toward their clear end, quietly, is you.

Make one line and carry it out. Mark something finished in a plain sentence and do the single thing the sentence asks for, the same day. A name can go in the sentence if the ending involves someone, and then the sentence is the whole move. When it's a clean cut, there is nothing left to keep hidden — no role to be seen in, no story to keep telling. The logic of endings can be carried out in one sentence, by the one doing it.

What ends cleanly doesn't need a keeper.
